evidence.text: The age of the environment taken for granted is long past, and now the world must fight determinedly for its future. One of the foremost impediments in that quest is the current destruction of rainforests. Deforestation poses catastrophic scenarios for the planet. It is singularly responsible for around a fifth of the world's carbon emissions. The vaporization of natural resources is inevitable. Millions of species become extinct – rain forests contain 50% of the earth’s entire pool. Rainfalls become unstable, atmospheric gases irregular. Thousands of indigenous people lose their habitat of centuries.

Our policy may seem limited, only targeting the reduction of destruction of rainforests. Yet, its implications are much more far-reaching, in the sense that it establishes a new trend for the UN’s attitude on climate change concerns by declaring that the days in which polluting as much as possible, as fast as possible, for quick money, are over. Until now, most countries have engaged in a neck-to-neck competition to consume as much resources as possible in order to achieve quick development, and common thought was that such governments were immune from facing the consequences of their rampant pollution. However, this sanction shows a fundamental change in attitude;

As we have already outlined, the propostion has grossly underestimated the effects of the proposed sanctions, and have gone completely unconsidered on the side of the importing countries. The greatest importers of these goods are the US and the EU countries. The US imports meat while the EU imports biofuel. So the countries in the UNSC, specially the US and France, would be highly unlikely to impose these sanction since this would have a direct effect on them due to shortages. It would be like punishing themselves.

These unprecedented sanctions will have far reaching effects. The receiving countries will be extremely angry since these products were demanded by many countries in UNSC, and suddenly, they themselves pass sanctions that will severly harm their economy. This will lead to bad relations not only between the countries but also between the UN and the countries. the solution that we have hihglighted is a much more peaceful one. The sanctions will also lead to the stagnation of development in many countries since the subsidies are unlikely to be enough.

No evidence establishes that sanctions would actually reduce deforestation or that the UN has the legal/practical means to impose them effectively. The claim is a normative policy prescription, but the dossier lacks sufficient evidence on overall effectiveness and trade-offs.

text.A|1:

However, material counterevidence undermines feasibility. E3 notes the largest importers of rainforest-linked goods are the US and EU; UNSC members would face domestic shortages and thus be unlikely to impose sanctions. These are empirical feasibility claims, not mere values. The dossier does not provide evidence that sanctions would be effective, enforceable, or that alternatives have failed. The claim may be desirable, but the supplied evidence is insufficient to establish it as workable policy.

Sanctions would directly harm these economies and punish the sanctioning countries themselves, creating severe diplomatic backlash and undermining development in targeted states. E4 also argues a more peaceful alternative exists. Thus, while the environmental urgency is clear, the dossier shows sanctions may be infeasible or counterproductive, not simply justified. The claim is a value judgment about the best policy; evidence supports urgency but not the sanction mechanism.

evidence.text: The age of the environment taken for granted is long past, and now the world must fight determinedly for its future. One of the foremost impediments in that quest is the current destruction of rainforests. Deforestation poses catastrophic scenarios for the planet. It is singularly responsible for around a fifth of the world's carbon emissions. The vaporization of natural resources is inevitable. Millions of species become extinct – rain forests contain 50% of the earth’s entire pool. Rainfalls become unstable, atmospheric gases irregular. Thousands of indigenous people lose their habitat of centuries.

Our policy may seem limited, only targeting the reduction of destruction of rainforests. Yet, its implications are much more far-reaching, in the sense that it establishes a new trend for the UN’s attitude on climate change concerns by declaring that the days in which polluting as much as possible, as fast as possible, for quick money, are over. Until now, most countries have engaged in a neck-to-neck competition to consume as much resources as possible in order to achieve quick development, and common thought was that such governments were immune from facing the consequences of their rampant pollution. However, this sanction shows a fundamental change in attitude;

As we have already outlined, the propostion has grossly underestimated the effects of the proposed sanctions, and have gone completely unconsidered on the side of the importing countries. The greatest importers of these goods are the US and the EU countries. The US imports meat while the EU imports biofuel. So the countries in the UNSC, specially the US and France, would be highly unlikely to impose these sanction since this would have a direct effect on them due to shortages. It would be like punishing themselves.

These unprecedented sanctions will have far reaching effects. The receiving countries will be extremely angry since these products were demanded by many countries in UNSC, and suddenly, they themselves pass sanctions that will severly harm their economy. This will lead to bad relations not only between the countries but also between the UN and the countries. the solution that we have hihglighted is a much more peaceful one. The sanctions will also lead to the stagnation of development in many countries since the subsidies are unlikely to be enough.

evidence.text: The age of the environment taken for granted is long past, and now the world must fight determinedly for its future. One of the foremost impediments in that quest is the current destruction of rainforests. Deforestation poses catastrophic scenarios for the planet. It is singularly responsible for around a fifth of the world's carbon emissions. The vaporization of natural resources is inevitable. Millions of species become extinct – rain forests contain 50% of the earth’s entire pool. Rainfalls become unstable, atmospheric gases irregular. Thousands of indigenous people lose their habitat of centuries.

Our policy may seem limited, only targeting the reduction of destruction of rainforests. Yet, its implications are much more far-reaching, in the sense that it establishes a new trend for the UN’s attitude on climate change concerns by declaring that the days in which polluting as much as possible, as fast as possible, for quick money, are over. Until now, most countries have engaged in a neck-to-neck competition to consume as much resources as possible in order to achieve quick development, and common thought was that such governments were immune from facing the consequences of their rampant pollution. However, this sanction shows a fundamental change in attitude;

As we have already outlined, the propostion has grossly underestimated the effects of the proposed sanctions, and have gone completely unconsidered on the side of the importing countries. The greatest importers of these goods are the US and the EU countries. The US imports meat while the EU imports biofuel. So the countries in the UNSC, specially the US and France, would be highly unlikely to impose these sanction since this would have a direct effect on them due to shortages. It would be like punishing themselves.

These unprecedented sanctions will have far reaching effects. The receiving countries will be extremely angry since these products were demanded by many countries in UNSC, and suddenly, they themselves pass sanctions that will severly harm their economy. This will lead to bad relations not only between the countries but also between the UN and the countries. the solution that we have hihglighted is a much more peaceful one. The sanctions will also lead to the stagnation of development in many countries since the subsidies are unlikely to be enough.

debates.claim: The UN should impose sanctions on countries that destroy their rainforests

text.A|1:
The dossier supports the factual urgency: deforestation drives ~20% of carbon emissions, threatens 50% of species, and destroys indigenous habitats. E2 indicates sanctions could signal a decisive UN shift against unchecked pollution.

However, material counterevidence undermines practical viability. E3 shows the largest importers—US and EU—would face shortages and thus are unlikely to impose sanctions, making the policy self-defeating. E4 warns sanctions would severely harm target economies, provoke anger, damage UN relations, and stall development, with inadequate subsidies.

Thus, while the moral/environmental case for action is strong, the dossier does not establish that sanctions are the effective or feasible mechanism. The claim mixes empirical benefits with contested value judgments about acceptable trade-offs.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.B|1:
The dossier supports the urgency of rainforest protection: E1 documents severe harms—20% of carbon emissions, species loss, and indigenous displacement. E2 also suggests sanctions could mark a needed shift in global environmental accountability.

However, the strongest countercase is practical and political. E3 shows the largest importers of rainforest-linked goods are the US and EU, meaning sanctions would directly harm the sanctioning powers themselves, making adoption implausible. E4 adds that targeted countries would face economic stagnation and diplomatic fallout, undermining the UN’s legitimacy and effectiveness. Thus, while the moral and environmental case is strong, the proposed mechanism appears counterproductive and infeasible as designed.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE
text.C|1:
The dossier establishes that rainforest destruction has severe environmental costs (E1), but it does not establish that UN sanctions are an appropriate or effective remedy. The claimed link between sanctions and reduced deforestation is asserted, not evidenced. E2 only describes a supposed shift in UN attitude; it provides no data showing sanctions change state behavior. E3 and E4 raise plausible objections—major importers would suffer, targeted countries would be harmed, development could stagnate—but these are speculative projections, not demonstrated outcomes. No evidence addresses whether sanctions would actually protect rainforests, whether they would be enforceable, or whether their costs would outweigh benefits. The claim is a value judgment about what the UN "should" do; the dossier supplies moral urgency and some policy risks, but not the empirical support needed to justify that prescription.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.A|2:
Panelist B correctly notes E3/E4 expose major political obstacles: the US and EU are top importers, so sanctions would self-harm and likely fail adoption. That undermines feasibility, but those objections are projections, not demonstrated outcomes.

Panelist C is stronger: the dossier gives no evidence that sanctions actually reduce deforestation. E1 establishes environmental harm, E2 only asserts a shift in UN attitude, and E3/E4 describe risks. The claim is a prescription, but the dossier lacks empirical support for effectiveness, enforceability, or cost-benefit balance. Moral urgency alone cannot justify the policy.

I therefore revise toward C: the case for urgency is solid, but the case for sanctions as the right tool is unsupported.

text.B|2:
Panelist A correctly identifies the tension: E1 and E2 show deforestation is catastrophic and sanctions could mark a needed shift. But their "uncertain" verdict underweights the concrete countercase. E3 states the largest importers—the US and EU—would directly suffer shortages, making the sanctions self-defeating and politically implausible. E4 adds that sanctions would severely damage recipient economies, inflame UN relations, and stall development, while noting a "more peaceful" alternative exists. No dossier evidence demonstrates sanctions would actually reduce deforestation or that their harms are justified. The supporting material establishes urgency, not that this specific coercive mechanism is sound. Therefore the claim is not merely unproven; the dossier actively undermines it.

text.C|2:

E3 shows the largest importers—US and EU—would face direct shortages and therefore have strong incentives to block sanctions, making the policy self-defeating. E4 adds concrete harms: severe economic damage to target countries, diplomatic fallout, and stalled development with inadequate subsidies. No evidence in the dossier shows sanctions would actually reduce deforestation or that these costs are justified. The claim is a policy prescription, not just a moral aspiration; given the demonstrated practical obstacles, the evidence undermines it.

No dossier evidence demonstrates that sanctions would reduce deforestation or that these costs are justified. The claim is a specific policy prescription, and the dossier affirmatively undercuts its feasibility and desirability.

text.B|3:

Moral urgency alone does not establish policy effectiveness.

Thus I agree with Panelist C and Panelist A’s revision: the harm case is solid, the sanctions case is unsupported.

E3/E4 describe political and economic risks—important, but projected, not demonstrated. The claim is a policy prescription, and no evidence supports its effectiveness, enforceability, or net benefit. Moral urgency alone cannot justify the specific tool. I therefore agree with Panelist A’s revised position: the problem is real, but the proposed remedy is unsupported by the dossier.

evidence.text: The age of the environment taken for granted is long past, and now the world must fight determinedly for its future. One of the foremost impediments in that quest is the current destruction of rainforests. Deforestation poses catastrophic scenarios for the planet. It is singularly responsible for around a fifth of the world's carbon emissions. The vaporization of natural resources is inevitable. Millions of species become extinct – rain forests contain 50% of the earth’s entire pool. Rainfalls become unstable, atmospheric gases irregular. Thousands of indigenous people lose their habitat of centuries.

Our policy may seem limited, only targeting the reduction of destruction of rainforests. Yet, its implications are much more far-reaching, in the sense that it establishes a new trend for the UN’s attitude on climate change concerns by declaring that the days in which polluting as much as possible, as fast as possible, for quick money, are over. Until now, most countries have engaged in a neck-to-neck competition to consume as much resources as possible in order to achieve quick development, and common thought was that such governments were immune from facing the consequences of their rampant pollution. However, this sanction shows a fundamental change in attitude;

As we have already outlined, the propostion has grossly underestimated the effects of the proposed sanctions, and have gone completely unconsidered on the side of the importing countries. The greatest importers of these goods are the US and the EU countries. The US imports meat while the EU imports biofuel. So the countries in the UNSC, specially the US and France, would be highly unlikely to impose these sanction since this would have a direct effect on them due to shortages. It would be like punishing themselves.

These unprecedented sanctions will have far reaching effects. The receiving countries will be extremely angry since these products were demanded by many countries in UNSC, and suddenly, they themselves pass sanctions that will severly harm their economy. This will lead to bad relations not only between the countries but also between the UN and the countries. the solution that we have hihglighted is a much more peaceful one. The sanctions will also lead to the stagnation of development in many countries since the subsidies are unlikely to be enough.

debates.claim: The UK Should Leave the European Union

text.A|1:
The dossier contains opinions and value judgments, not causal evidence. E1 asserts UK “cherry-picks” EU membership but provides no data on commitments. E2 claims UK taxes go to other EU states and that exit would improve trade and employment, but offers no figures or comparisons. E3 notes tuition differences and EU student access, yet does not link EU membership to UK fee levels. E4 argues international fees subsidise UK students, but does not address EU exit specifically. No source establishes net economic, social, or political effects of leaving. The claim is normative (“should leave”), and the evidence cannot support or refute it empirically.  
VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.B|1:
The dossier is mostly opinion and value judgments, not systematic evidence. E1 asserts the UK “blew it” over the euro and treats the EU like a menu—this is a rhetorical preference, not a fact. E2 claims UK taxpayers give “huge amounts” to Europe and that leaving would enable self-sufficiency and better trade, but provides no figures, comparisons, or causal analysis. E3 notes tuition differences and Denmark’s free places for EU students, implying EU membership benefits UK students abroad—this could cut against leaving. E4 argues international fees subsidize UK students, but does not address EU fees specifically or Brexit effects. No evidence covers trade losses, regulatory costs, migration impacts, or net budget contributions rigorously. The claim may be plausible to some, but the dossier lacks the empirical basis to support it.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.C|1:
The dossier mainly offers opinion and selective anecdotes, not systematic evidence. E2 asserts UK taxpayer money flows to other EU states without net contribution figures or counterfactual trade analysis. E3’s tuition comparison ignores reciprocal Erasmus/study arrangements and broader EU benefits. E4 actually undercuts E3 by noting international student fees subsidize UK students, but it does not directly address EU membership. No evidence covers regulatory trade-offs, sovereignty, security, migration, or alternative trade agreements. The claim is normative, and the supporting reasons are incomplete and sometimes contradictory. External validity is weak: individual examples (Denmark, Polish labor) are overgeneralized to the entire EU relationship. Missing conditions include post-exit transition costs, new trade barriers, and regional impacts. Therefore, the available evidence cannot support a firm conclusion.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.A|2:
The dossier contains opinions and assertions, not rigorous causal evidence. E2 claims UK taxpayers’ money goes to other EU governments and that leaving would improve UK employment and trade, but no data or counterfactual analysis is supplied. E1 and E3 discuss EU policies and access to education/labor but do not establish net effects of membership. E4 actually supports staying in the EU or maintaining international students, showing higher fees subsidize UK students, but it does not directly test the leave/remain question. The claim is normative (“should leave”), and the evidence only offers selected, unquantified grievances and benefits. No reliable causal link from EU membership to UK economic or social outcomes is demonstrated.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.B|2:

E4 actually suggests international fees help UK students, yet it does not model leaving the EU. The claim is a normative prescription; the evidence cannot empirically support or refute it. No revision is warranted.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN

Panelist B correctly identifies missing evidence on trade, regulation, migration, and net contributions. No rigorous data supports the claim that leaving would improve UK welfare. The available concrete claims are anecdotal and partially countervailing. Therefore the dossier is insufficient to either support or undermine the claim.

evidence.text: In for a penny in for a pound .. or not... The UK chose not to commit to the single currency and has been treating the EU like a restaurant menu . The UK should do the decent thing and leave. It's too late to commit fully , you had your chances , you blew it. When it comes to making contracts for business ventures , making allowances for education abroad , businesses etc have been making allowances and have been including UK businesses . That general way of thinking should just change. Polish and other eastern European labor is a lot cheaper for western European countries .

Although Britain is in a bit of a bad state as it is, British taxes are still being used to give other European governments huge amounts of money. Unemployment is up and our country appears to be coasting, desperately avoiding a double dip recession. If we could withdraw Britain from the EU, become self-sufficient and start trade routes with other countries we could be so much better. Instead, our taxpayers money is being used to pay for other Europeans rather than British nationals. It is depriving British people of work and advantages which they ought to have.

British students may have to pay up to £9,000 a year next year for tuition. In most EU countries it is either cheaper, or in Denmark's case, free. The Danes are only letting Brits study there because Britain is in the EU. The the issue of the meal ticket. Where is the problem with that as long as they pay their taxes ? And the British didn't do that ? India, Canada, Australia, New Zeland, Hong Kong, Jamaica. Where do you think that British got their riches from ?

The cost of higher education in the UK is far greater than the amount a UK student pays. Without the higher fees that come from international students, UK students would be paying a lot more than they are, which would be bad for several reasons. Firstly, it would lower the numbers of UK students who go to university, particularly from poorer backgrounds. Education is the best way to get out of poverty, so keeping poor people out of education is self-evidently a bad thing. Secondly, and consequently, it would lower the number of graduates in the job market.

debates.claim: The UK Should Leave the European Union

text.A|1:
The dossier provides mostly opinion and anecdotal assertions, not robust evidence. E1 and E2 claim UK taxpayers subsidise other EU states and that leaving would enable self-sufficiency and new trade routes, but no figures or comparative analysis are supplied. E3 notes tuition cost differences and Danish access for Brits due to EU membership, implying benefits of staying. Material counterevidence appears in E4: international students’ higher fees subsidise UK students; leaving the EU could reduce international student numbers, raising UK fees and reducing access for poorer students. This directly undermines the leave case on education grounds. The claim is ultimately a value judgment—"should leave"—not a factual statement. The empirical fragments point both ways, but the dossier lacks sufficient data to resolve the trade-offs. Therefore, the claim cannot be supported or undermined on this evidence.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.B|1:
The dossier contains no authoritative economic or legal analysis, only opinionated excerpts. The strongest countercase to leaving is [E4]: UK students benefit from higher international fees subsidising domestic tuition, and leaving the EU could reduce that cross-subsidy, harming poorer students and the graduate pipeline. [E3] also notes EU membership enables Britons to study in countries like Denmark for free, undermining the leave case. Material supporting evidence is weak: [E1] and [E2] assert that EU payments and labour competition harm Britain, but offer no data on net contributions, trade alternatives, or employment effects. [E3] mixes colonial nostalgia with tuition complaints. Overall, the dossier is anecdotal, contradictory, and value-laden; it cannot resolve the complex cost-benefit question of EU membership.  

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.C|1:
The claim is a value judgment, but the dossier’s supporting evidence is weak. E1 asserts the UK "cherry-picks" and should leave, but provides no empirical basis for why that requires exit. E2 claims leaving would allow self-sufficiency and better trade, and that UK taxes "pay for other Europeans" rather than Britons—these are empirical links asserted without data. E3 discusses tuition fees and Danish access, but does not establish that leaving the EU would improve UK education or that EU membership causes harm. E4 actually suggests international students (including EU students) subsidise UK higher education, which could undermine a leave argument, but it does not directly address EU membership. No evidence establishes causation between EU membership and the UK’s economic or educational problems, nor that exit would produce the claimed benefits. The asserted links—EU membership causing financial loss, preventing trade, or harming students—are not established. The dossier contains opinions and anecdotes, not verified facts.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.A|2:
The dossier contains no rigorous cost-benefit analysis; most entries are opinionated assertions rather than evidence. E1 and E2 express value judgments that UK tax contributions are excessive and that self-sufficiency would improve outcomes—but provide no data on net trade effects, budget balances, or employment impacts. E3 illustrates an EU benefit: UK students access cheaper or free education in Denmark, implying leaving could reduce such opportunities. Material counterevidence appears in E4: international student fees subsidise UK higher education, so reduced international enrolment—potentially from leaving the EU—could raise costs for UK students and reduce access. Thus the claim rests on selective arguments, with both potential gains and losses acknowledged but not quantified. The normative claim "should leave" cannot be resolved from this dossier.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.B|2:
I concur with Panelist A’s assessment. E4 is the only concrete empirical counterweight: international students’ higher fees subsidise UK domestic students, so leaving the EU could reduce that subsidy, raise fees, and hit poorer students hardest. That is a material harm to the leave case.

E1 and E2, by contrast, offer no figures on net UK budget contributions, trade diversion, or employment effects—they are assertions, not evidence. E3 cuts both ways: EU membership gives British students access to cheaper or free tuition abroad, but also highlights UK domestic fee inequality. No dossier evidence quantifies overall economic or welfare effects of leaving.

The claim is ultimately a normative judgment, and the empirical fragments are too thin to resolve it. Panelist A’s reasoning stands; I see no warrant to revise.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.C|2:
Panelist B correctly notes the dossier lacks economic or legal analysis. I would sharpen one point: [E4] does not establish a link between EU membership and international-fee cross-subsidies, since international students come largely from outside the EU. So it is not a strong countercase to leaving. [E3] asserts that EU membership lets Britons study in Denmark for free, but provides no evidence on numbers, costs, or whether this would end after Brexit. [E1] and [E2] assert that EU payments and Eastern European labour harm UK jobs and taxpayers, but provide no data on net contributions, wage effects, or alternative trade arrangements. These are asserted links, not established facts. The remaining material is value-laden opinion about what Britain "should" do. The dossier cannot resolve the complex empirical trade-offs, so the claim remains unsupported.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.A|3:

debates.claim: The UK Should Leave the European Union

text.A|1:
The dossier contains some concrete empirical claims but no comprehensive evidence on the overall effects of leaving the EU.

Supporting leave: E2 claims the UK is a net contributor to EU budgets and that taxpayer funds could instead be spent domestically. E1 notes the UK already has opt-outs from the euro and treats EU membership selectively.

Supporting remain: E3 states British students can access cheaper or free university education in some EU countries because of EU membership. E4 argues international students’ fees subsidise UK higher education; if leaving reduced those students, UK fees could rise. However, E4 does not directly tie this to EU membership.

The claim itself is a value judgment, not a factual statement. The evidence addresses narrow points but lacks data on trade, jobs, regulation, or long-term economic effects. Therefore the dossier is insufficient to support a firm conclusion.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.B|1:
The dossier consists largely of value judgments and unsupported assertions, not verifiable evidence. E1 asserts the UK cherry-picks EU membership and should leave; E2 claims UK taxpayers’ money goes to other EU states and that withdrawal would improve trade—but provides no figures on net contributions, employment effects, or trade alternatives. E3 mixes a factual claim about UK tuition fees with an emotive argument about EU access and colonial history. E4 argues international students subsidize UK students, which actually supports remaining open—but does not directly address EU membership. No source provides economic, legal, or political data sufficient to adjudicate the normative claim that the UK should leave. The dossier offers opinions and anecdotes, not empirical proof. On this evidence, the claim cannot be supported or undermined.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.C|1:
The dossier contains both supportive and critical arguments, but no comprehensive evidence to resolve the claim.

Supporting Leave: E1 argues the UK’s opt-outs make membership incoherent; E2 claims UK taxpayer money transfers to other EU governments and that leaving could enable new trade routes.

Undermining Leave: E3 notes EU membership gives British students access to cheaper or free tuition in other member states; E4 argues international student fees subsidise UK students, implying reduced access after exit could harm poorer students and graduate numbers.

These are largely value judgments and selective empirical claims. No data are supplied on net budget contributions, trade effects, or student flows. The claim is normative, and the dossier cannot establish whether leaving would improve UK welfare overall.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.A|2:
Both prior assessments are sound. The dossier contains no reliable data on UK net EU contributions, trade diversion, employment effects, or student flows. E1 and E2 assert that leaving would improve self-sufficiency and trade, but provide no figures. E3 notes a concrete tuition differential and EU access, yet does not quantify how exit would affect student mobility. E4 suggests international fees subsidise UK students—relevant to openness, but not directly to EU membership. These are mostly value judgments and selective anecdotes, not empirical proof. The normative claim that the UK should leave cannot be confirmed or refuted on this record.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.B|2:
Panelist A correctly distinguishes factual claims from the value judgment underlying the claim. E2 asserts that UK taxpayer money goes to other EU governments and could be spent domestically, but provides no budget figures or comparison with trade benefits. E1 notes UK opt-outs, which is a factual observation but does not establish that leaving is better. E3 and E4 raise concrete points about higher education: EU membership enables UK students to study cheaply in some EU states, and international student fees subsidise UK domestic fees. However, E4 does not link those students specifically to EU membership. The dossier lacks evidence on trade, regulation, jobs, or long-term economic consequences. The claim remains a policy preference, not a conclusion the evidence can settle.

text.C|2:

evidence.text: In for a penny in for a pound .. or not... The UK chose not to commit to the single currency and has been treating the EU like a restaurant menu . The UK should do the decent thing and leave. It's too late to commit fully , you had your chances , you blew it. When it comes to making contracts for business ventures , making allowances for education abroad , businesses etc have been making allowances and have been including UK businesses . That general way of thinking should just change. Polish and other eastern European labor is a lot cheaper for western European countries .

Although Britain is in a bit of a bad state as it is, British taxes are still being used to give other European governments huge amounts of money. Unemployment is up and our country appears to be coasting, desperately avoiding a double dip recession. If we could withdraw Britain from the EU, become self-sufficient and start trade routes with other countries we could be so much better. Instead, our taxpayers money is being used to pay for other Europeans rather than British nationals. It is depriving British people of work and advantages which they ought to have.

British students may have to pay up to £9,000 a year next year for tuition. In most EU countries it is either cheaper, or in Denmark's case, free. The Danes are only letting Brits study there because Britain is in the EU. The the issue of the meal ticket. Where is the problem with that as long as they pay their taxes ? And the British didn't do that ? India, Canada, Australia, New Zeland, Hong Kong, Jamaica. Where do you think that British got their riches from ?

The cost of higher education in the UK is far greater than the amount a UK student pays. Without the higher fees that come from international students, UK students would be paying a lot more than they are, which would be bad for several reasons. Firstly, it would lower the numbers of UK students who go to university, particularly from poorer backgrounds. Education is the best way to get out of poverty, so keeping poor people out of education is self-evidently a bad thing. Secondly, and consequently, it would lower the number of graduates in the job market.

evidence.text: In a free society individuals should be able to do as they wish unless their actions harm others, even if their actions harm themselves. This does not mean that with the legalization of recreational drugs should come a completely hands off approach. Education about the effects of recreational drugs, safe and controlled environments in which to consume recreational drugs, monitoring of strict standards that recreational drugs must meet in order to be sold, and other measures which ensure the consumption of recreational drugs is informed, safe, and controlled should be implemented.

The proposition team believes that the victims of low-quality drugs will be lowered to a much smaller number than the number of victims nowadays. And the reason why this will happen is not only that there are not going to be new addicts, but that drugs are going to be purified. We believe that overdoses and impure drugs are the main reasons for people to die from drugs. As we all know there is no dealer who will tell his customers that by buying this product they threaten their health or that there are special programs which help people to stop using drugs.

Romney also has a record of preferring prohibitory policies over those that allow drug use with the intention of making it safer. For example, as Governor of Massachusetts, he vetoed a bill to allow the sale of syringes without a prescription. Romney has staunchly opposed calls to legalize and regulate marijuana, making a moral argument against such a change by claiming that pot legalization is simply a pet issue of a “pleasure-seeking generation that never grew up.” While President Obama has not supported the legalization of marijuana, Romney is stronger in calling for harsh penalties for marijuana users in order to demonstrate the seriousness of the crime.

Like Obama, Romney has indicated a willingness to talk to Mexican leaders about collaboration and has admitted the need to address large-scale demand for drugs in the United States. When asked how to improve the War on Drugs, he stated, “We gotta stop the demand here in this country.” And that demand is immense, it is estimated that there are 22.6 million Americans aged 12 of over using illegal drugs. Through education and regulation, the United States can win the War on Drugs, rather than appease drug growers, traffickers, dealers, and users. Rockville, MD: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 2011.

debates.claim: The Illegality Of Recreational Drugs Does More Harm Than Good

text.A|1:
The dossier offers normative arguments (E1) and a causal claim (E2) that prohibition increases deaths from impure drugs and overdoses, but it provides no comparative data on harm reduction. E4 cites 22.6 million users and calls for education/regulation, yet does not measure prohibition’s net effects. Counterevidence appears in E3: a political record favoring prohibition and harsh penalties, which implies a belief that illegality deters use—though this is a value stance, not empirical proof. No source quantifies harms of illegality versus legalization, nor controls for confounding factors. Thus the claim rests on plausible reasoning, not dossier-supported evidence. The material is insufficient to establish that illegality does more harm than good.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.B|1:
The dossier provides direct support for the claim. E1 argues that a free society should permit drug use with regulation, implying prohibition is an unjustified restriction. E2 asserts that illegality causes deaths from overdoses and impure drugs because dealers lack incentives to warn users, and that legal regulation would reduce harm. These are empirical claims about harm caused by prohibition.

The strongest countercase is weak. E3 and E4 document political opposition to legalization, including moral arguments and support for the War on Drugs, but they offer no evidence that illegality reduces harm or does good. E4 acknowledges immense demand and proposes education and regulation—not prohibition—as the solution, which actually aligns with the claim. No dossier source demonstrates that criminalization improves health or safety outcomes.

VERDICT: SUPPORT
text.C|1:
The claim is an empirical causal assertion: that criminalization produces more net harm than legalization with regulation. The dossier does not establish this.

E1 is a value argument about liberty, not evidence of outcomes. E2 asserts that legalization would reduce overdose deaths and addiction, but provides no comparative data, and assumes without support that legal markets would be pure, regulated, and effectively educational. E3 and E4 describe political positions and demand statistics; they do not test the claim that illegality itself causes greater harm than legal regulation. No evidence compares actual harm under prohibition versus legalization, nor measures “good” versus “harm” in comparable terms.

Thus the asserted causal links—between illegality and net harm, and between legalization and improved safety—are not established by the dossier.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.A|2:
The dossier offers partial support for the claim. E2 provides empirical reasoning: prohibition leaves drug quality unregulated, causing overdoses and deaths from impure substances, while dealers provide no safety information. E1 adds a value argument favoring legalization with regulation, education, and controlled environments.

However, the dossier lacks systematic evidence on the total harms of illegality versus legalization. E3 is material counterevidence only in showing political opposition to harm-reduction measures, not in showing illegality does more good. E4 shifts focus to demand reduction and education, which is compatible with either policy.

The claim is plausible but not established. No data quantify deaths, addiction rates, or black-market effects. The dossier mixes value judgments with limited empirical assertions.

No dossier evidence quantifies how many deaths or harms are caused by illegality versus how many are prevented by deterrence. E3 offers only political stances favoring prohibition—a value judgment, not empirical proof of net benefit. Thus the claim is plausible but unsupported by controlled data or cost-benefit analysis. I retain UNCERTAIN rather than UNDERMINE because E2 and E4 give real, if incomplete, empirical grounding.

evidence.text: In a free society individuals should be able to do as they wish unless their actions harm others, even if their actions harm themselves. This does not mean that with the legalization of recreational drugs should come a completely hands off approach. Education about the effects of recreational drugs, safe and controlled environments in which to consume recreational drugs, monitoring of strict standards that recreational drugs must meet in order to be sold, and other measures which ensure the consumption of recreational drugs is informed, safe, and controlled should be implemented.

The proposition team believes that the victims of low-quality drugs will be lowered to a much smaller number than the number of victims nowadays. And the reason why this will happen is not only that there are not going to be new addicts, but that drugs are going to be purified. We believe that overdoses and impure drugs are the main reasons for people to die from drugs. As we all know there is no dealer who will tell his customers that by buying this product they threaten their health or that there are special programs which help people to stop using drugs.

Romney also has a record of preferring prohibitory policies over those that allow drug use with the intention of making it safer. For example, as Governor of Massachusetts, he vetoed a bill to allow the sale of syringes without a prescription. Romney has staunchly opposed calls to legalize and regulate marijuana, making a moral argument against such a change by claiming that pot legalization is simply a pet issue of a “pleasure-seeking generation that never grew up.” While President Obama has not supported the legalization of marijuana, Romney is stronger in calling for harsh penalties for marijuana users in order to demonstrate the seriousness of the crime.

Like Obama, Romney has indicated a willingness to talk to Mexican leaders about collaboration and has admitted the need to address large-scale demand for drugs in the United States. When asked how to improve the War on Drugs, he stated, “We gotta stop the demand here in this country.” And that demand is immense, it is estimated that there are 22.6 million Americans aged 12 of over using illegal drugs. Through education and regulation, the United States can win the War on Drugs, rather than appease drug growers, traffickers, dealers, and users. Rockville, MD: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 2011.

The dossier contains mostly value claims and political positions, not empirical evidence about net harms.

E1 argues a free society should allow self-harm and regulate drugs; this is a normative claim, not evidence of outcomes. E2 asserts legalization would reduce deaths from overdoses and impure drugs, but offers no data or causal analysis. E3 and E4 describe political stances and drug-demand estimates; they do not test whether prohibition causes more harm than good.

No controlled comparisons, mortality data, addiction rates, or black-market analyses are supplied. Therefore the claim is not established by the evidence.

evidence.text: In a free society individuals should be able to do as they wish unless their actions harm others, even if their actions harm themselves. This does not mean that with the legalization of recreational drugs should come a completely hands off approach. Education about the effects of recreational drugs, safe and controlled environments in which to consume recreational drugs, monitoring of strict standards that recreational drugs must meet in order to be sold, and other measures which ensure the consumption of recreational drugs is informed, safe, and controlled should be implemented.

The proposition team believes that the victims of low-quality drugs will be lowered to a much smaller number than the number of victims nowadays. And the reason why this will happen is not only that there are not going to be new addicts, but that drugs are going to be purified. We believe that overdoses and impure drugs are the main reasons for people to die from drugs. As we all know there is no dealer who will tell his customers that by buying this product they threaten their health or that there are special programs which help people to stop using drugs.

Romney also has a record of preferring prohibitory policies over those that allow drug use with the intention of making it safer. For example, as Governor of Massachusetts, he vetoed a bill to allow the sale of syringes without a prescription. Romney has staunchly opposed calls to legalize and regulate marijuana, making a moral argument against such a change by claiming that pot legalization is simply a pet issue of a “pleasure-seeking generation that never grew up.” While President Obama has not supported the legalization of marijuana, Romney is stronger in calling for harsh penalties for marijuana users in order to demonstrate the seriousness of the crime.

Like Obama, Romney has indicated a willingness to talk to Mexican leaders about collaboration and has admitted the need to address large-scale demand for drugs in the United States. When asked how to improve the War on Drugs, he stated, “We gotta stop the demand here in this country.” And that demand is immense, it is estimated that there are 22.6 million Americans aged 12 of over using illegal drugs. Through education and regulation, the United States can win the War on Drugs, rather than appease drug growers, traffickers, dealers, and users. Rockville, MD: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 2011.

debates.claim: The Illegality Of Recreational Drugs Does More Harm Than Good

text.A|1:
The strongest dossier-based case: E2 argues prohibition’s main harms are overdoses and deaths from impure, unregulated drugs; legalization with quality standards would reduce those deaths. E4 shows the policy has failed to curb massive demand (22.6 million users), suggesting criminalization is not working. E1 adds that regulated legalization—with education and safety controls—can address harm without endorsing use.

Material counterevidence: E3 shows influential policymakers prefer prohibition on moral grounds, and one opposed even harm-reduction measures like syringe access. That indicates political resistance, but it does not demonstrate that illegality produces net benefits. The dossier lacks direct data comparing prohibition’s benefits (e.g., deterrence, reduced use) to its harms.

On the available evidence, the claim is supported more than undermined, though the comparison is not fully quantified.

VERDICT: SUPPORT
text.B|1:
The dossier provides partial support for the claim. E1 and E2 argue that legalization with regulation would reduce deaths from impure drugs and enable education and safe environments—empirical claims about harm reduction. However, the strongest countercase comes from E3 and E4, which defend prohibition on moral grounds and advocate reducing demand through education and enforcement rather than legalization. E3’s moral argument is a value judgment, not evidence; E4’s claim that the War on Drugs can be "won" is an assertion without outcome data. No dossier evidence directly measures whether illegality causes more harm than good—no data on addiction rates, overdose deaths, black-market violence, or enforcement costs under prohibition versus legalization. Thus, while E1 and E2 support the claim, the dossier lacks sufficient empirical comparison to settle it.  
VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.C|1:
The dossier does not establish the claim. E1 is a value judgment about liberty and regulation, not evidence of net harm. E2 asserts that legalization would reduce deaths from overdoses and impure drugs, but provides no data, comparison, or causal evidence; it also assumes addiction rates would not rise. E3 and E4 discuss political positions and general War on Drugs rhetoric, but do not measure harms or benefits of illegality. The specific link between illegality and greater net harm—including effects on addiction, public health, crime, and personal freedom—is asserted, not demonstrated. No empirical comparison is supplied.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.A|2:
I concur with Panelist C more than Panelist B. E1 is purely normative—it asserts liberty and regulation, not measurable outcomes. E2 makes concrete empirical claims: legalization would reduce overdose deaths and harms from impure drugs. But it offers no data, no baseline, and no comparison of addiction or black-market effects; it also assumes no rise in new addicts. E3 and E4 are political stances and moral/value judgments, not evidence of net harm or benefit. Panelist B calls E1/E2 “partial support,” but support requires empirical grounding. The dossier never quantifies harms caused by illegality—overdose rates, enforcement costs, cartel violence—versus harms of legalization. Thus the claim remains asserted, not demonstrated. No revision is warranted beyond strengthening the conclusion.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.B|2:
Panelist A’s supporting case rests on E2’s mechanism—impure drugs and overdoses under prohibition—and E4’s evidence of 22.6 million users despite criminalization. Those are material: they identify plausible harms and show prohibition has not eliminated demand.

However, the dossier lacks comparative data. E2 is an assertion (“we believe”), not measured outcomes. E4 shows demand but not that illegality causes more harm than good; it could also imply enforcement reduces use below what legalization would bring. E1 is a value argument, not empirical evidence. E3 shows political resistance and even opposition to syringe access, but that reflects moral judgments, not net effects.

The strongest countercase is therefore evidentiary insufficiency: the claim requires comparing prohibition’s harms (deaths, black markets) against its benefits (deterrence, reduced use), and the dossier provides no quantified comparison. Supporting mechanisms exist, but they do not establish net harm.

That asserted causal link is not established. E4 shows 22.6 million users, indicating prohibition has not eliminated demand, but it does not measure prohibition’s benefits—deterrence, treatment referrals, or reduced availability—so it cannot support a net-harm comparison. E1 is a value preference for liberty and regulated access, not empirical evidence of net outcomes. E3 only documents political and moral opposition, including opposition to syringe access; it neither supports nor refutes the claim. The dossier lacks comparative evidence on the harms of illegality versus the good of prohibition. Therefore the claim that illegality does more harm than good is not established on this record.

evidence.text: In a free society individuals should be able to do as they wish unless their actions harm others, even if their actions harm themselves. This does not mean that with the legalization of recreational drugs should come a completely hands off approach. Education about the effects of recreational drugs, safe and controlled environments in which to consume recreational drugs, monitoring of strict standards that recreational drugs must meet in order to be sold, and other measures which ensure the consumption of recreational drugs is informed, safe, and controlled should be implemented.

The proposition team believes that the victims of low-quality drugs will be lowered to a much smaller number than the number of victims nowadays. And the reason why this will happen is not only that there are not going to be new addicts, but that drugs are going to be purified. We believe that overdoses and impure drugs are the main reasons for people to die from drugs. As we all know there is no dealer who will tell his customers that by buying this product they threaten their health or that there are special programs which help people to stop using drugs.

Romney also has a record of preferring prohibitory policies over those that allow drug use with the intention of making it safer. For example, as Governor of Massachusetts, he vetoed a bill to allow the sale of syringes without a prescription. Romney has staunchly opposed calls to legalize and regulate marijuana, making a moral argument against such a change by claiming that pot legalization is simply a pet issue of a “pleasure-seeking generation that never grew up.” While President Obama has not supported the legalization of marijuana, Romney is stronger in calling for harsh penalties for marijuana users in order to demonstrate the seriousness of the crime.

Like Obama, Romney has indicated a willingness to talk to Mexican leaders about collaboration and has admitted the need to address large-scale demand for drugs in the United States. When asked how to improve the War on Drugs, he stated, “We gotta stop the demand here in this country.” And that demand is immense, it is estimated that there are 22.6 million Americans aged 12 of over using illegal drugs. Through education and regulation, the United States can win the War on Drugs, rather than appease drug growers, traffickers, dealers, and users. Rockville, MD: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 2011.

evidence.text: The May 2014 National Climate Assessment report said human-caused climate changes, such as increased heat waves and drought, "are visible in every state." A Sep. 2014 American Meteorological Society study found that human-caused climate change "greatly increased" (up to 10 times) the risk for extreme heat waves in 2013. According to an Aug. 2012 study published in the , there is a "high degree of confidence" that the Texas and Oklahoma heat waves and drought of 2011, and heat waves and drought in Moscow in 2010, "were a consequence of global warming" and that "extreme anomalies" in weather are becoming more common as a direct consequence of human-caused climate change.

According to The Center For Biological Diversity , the world's climate is changing as a result of the burning of fossil fuels. The burning of fossil fuels creates carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide traps heat in the atmosphere, and this causes the world's temperature to rise. This is likely to reduce the amount of arable land on Earth, and it will cause food prices to increase. Furthermore, climate change is likely to result in rising sea levels. There even are major cities that could be flooded. As the population increases, the production of fossil fuels will increase. This is likely to result in climate change occurring at an increasingly rapid pace.

It is the sun that is the driving force of our climate and so it makes sense that it has the biggest impact on our climate rather than anything that humans might be doing. The sun is therefore the most likely cause of global warming. Professor Henrik Svensmark, a physicist at the Danish National Space Center in Copenhagen argues that climate change is caused by solar activity. Solar activity could affect climate by variation in the Sun's output or potentially through having an effect on cloud formation. Sunspot numbers and cosmic ray fluxes...

Over the past 10,000 years, solar minima (reduced sun spot activity) have been "accompanied by sharp climate changes." Between 1900 and 2000 solar irradiance increased 0.19%, and correlated with the rise in US surface temperatures over the 20th century. According to a 2007 study published in , "variations in solar activity and not the burning of fossil fuels are the direct cause of the observed multiyear variations in climatic responses." In a 2012 study by Willie Soon, PhD, Physicist at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, a strong correlation between solar radiation and temperatures in the Arctic over the past 130 years was identified.

Counter-evidence (E3, E4) attributes climate change to solar activity, citing correlations between solar irradiance/sunspots and temperature, and a 2012 Arctic correlation study. However, these sources offer correlation and a single physicist's argument, not direct refutation of the attribution studies in E1. evidence.text: The May 2014 National Climate Assessment report said human-caused climate changes, such as increased heat waves and drought, "are visible in every state." A Sep. 2014 American Meteorological Society study found that human-caused climate change "greatly increased" (up to 10 times) the risk for extreme heat waves in 2013. According to an Aug. 2012 study published in the , there is a "high degree of confidence" that the Texas and Oklahoma heat waves and drought of 2011, and heat waves and drought in Moscow in 2010, "were a consequence of global warming" and that "extreme anomalies" in weather are becoming more common as a direct consequence of human-caused climate change.

According to The Center For Biological Diversity , the world's climate is changing as a result of the burning of fossil fuels. The burning of fossil fuels creates carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide traps heat in the atmosphere, and this causes the world's temperature to rise. This is likely to reduce the amount of arable land on Earth, and it will cause food prices to increase. Furthermore, climate change is likely to result in rising sea levels. There even are major cities that could be flooded. As the population increases, the production of fossil fuels will increase. This is likely to result in climate change occurring at an increasingly rapid pace.

It is the sun that is the driving force of our climate and so it makes sense that it has the biggest impact on our climate rather than anything that humans might be doing. The sun is therefore the most likely cause of global warming. Professor Henrik Svensmark, a physicist at the Danish National Space Center in Copenhagen argues that climate change is caused by solar activity. Solar activity could affect climate by variation in the Sun's output or potentially through having an effect on cloud formation. Sunspot numbers and cosmic ray fluxes...

Over the past 10,000 years, solar minima (reduced sun spot activity) have been "accompanied by sharp climate changes." Between 1900 and 2000 solar irradiance increased 0.19%, and correlated with the rise in US surface temperatures over the 20th century. According to a 2007 study published in , "variations in solar activity and not the burning of fossil fuels are the direct cause of the observed multiyear variations in climatic responses." In a 2012 study by Willie Soon, PhD, Physicist at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, a strong correlation between solar radiation and temperatures in the Arctic over the past 130 years was identified.

E2 outlines concrete, observable risks: reduced arable land, rising food prices, sea-level rise, and flooding of major cities. These are empirical projections, not value judgments.

Counterevidence exists: E3 and E4 attribute warming to solar activity, citing correlations and a physicist's argument. However, correlation does not establish causation, and these sources do not refute the documented human fingerprint on recent extremes. The claim that the threat is "exaggerated" requires showing impacts are overstated; the dossier instead shows severe, measurable risks.

Value judgments about acceptable risk aside, the empirical record in E1–E2 indicates the threat is substantial, not exaggerated.

evidence.text: The May 2014 National Climate Assessment report said human-caused climate changes, such as increased heat waves and drought, "are visible in every state." A Sep. 2014 American Meteorological Society study found that human-caused climate change "greatly increased" (up to 10 times) the risk for extreme heat waves in 2013. According to an Aug. 2012 study published in the , there is a "high degree of confidence" that the Texas and Oklahoma heat waves and drought of 2011, and heat waves and drought in Moscow in 2010, "were a consequence of global warming" and that "extreme anomalies" in weather are becoming more common as a direct consequence of human-caused climate change.

According to The Center For Biological Diversity , the world's climate is changing as a result of the burning of fossil fuels. The burning of fossil fuels creates carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide traps heat in the atmosphere, and this causes the world's temperature to rise. This is likely to reduce the amount of arable land on Earth, and it will cause food prices to increase. Furthermore, climate change is likely to result in rising sea levels. There even are major cities that could be flooded. As the population increases, the production of fossil fuels will increase. This is likely to result in climate change occurring at an increasingly rapid pace.

It is the sun that is the driving force of our climate and so it makes sense that it has the biggest impact on our climate rather than anything that humans might be doing. The sun is therefore the most likely cause of global warming. Professor Henrik Svensmark, a physicist at the Danish National Space Center in Copenhagen argues that climate change is caused by solar activity. Solar activity could affect climate by variation in the Sun's output or potentially through having an effect on cloud formation. Sunspot numbers and cosmic ray fluxes...

Over the past 10,000 years, solar minima (reduced sun spot activity) have been "accompanied by sharp climate changes." Between 1900 and 2000 solar irradiance increased 0.19%, and correlated with the rise in US surface temperatures over the 20th century. According to a 2007 study published in , "variations in solar activity and not the burning of fossil fuels are the direct cause of the observed multiyear variations in climatic responses." In a 2012 study by Willie Soon, PhD, Physicist at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, a strong correlation between solar radiation and temperatures in the Arctic over the past 130 years was identified.

E2 identifies specific physical mechanisms and risks—CO₂-driven warming, sea-level rise, reduced arable land—though it also includes projections that are partly value-laden. E3 and E4 offer only correlations between solar activity and temperature; they do not quantify the human contribution or show that climate threats are overstated. Panelists B and C correctly note that solar correlation can coexist with a significant human role and does not refute the documented impacts. The dossier’s strongest empirical evidence supports a serious, measurable threat, not an exaggerated one.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE
text.B|3:
The evidence still undercuts the claim. E1 provides attribution studies with high confidence linking specific heat waves and droughts to human-caused warming—not speculation. E2 identifies a concrete mechanism: fossil-fuel CO₂ traps heat, with projected effects on arable land, food prices, and sea-level rise.

E3 and E4 do not refute this. They show correlations between solar activity and temperature, but correlation is not causation. A 0.19% irradiance increase over the 20th century is not shown to account for observed warming trends, and the cited studies do not quantify the threat or dispute the attribution findings in E1. At most, they suggest some scientific uncertainty about solar influences—but uncertainty about mechanisms does not demonstrate exaggeration.

The claim is a value judgment, but the dossier’s empirical evidence supports substantial, human-linked climate risks. No revision is warranted.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE
text.C|3:
The dossier’s strongest evidence still contradicts the claim. E1 provides specific attribution studies with high confidence linking human-caused warming to extreme heat and drought events. E2 identifies a concrete causal mechanism—CO₂ trapping heat—with downstream risks to food supply and coastal cities. These are empirical claims, not value judgments.

E3 and E4 offer only correlations between solar activity and temperature. Correlation does not establish causation, and neither source quantifies the overall threat or directly rebuts the attribution findings in E1. At most, they indicate unresolved questions about some mechanisms. Uncertainty about solar influences does not demonstrate that the climate threat is exaggerated.

The claim remains a value judgment, but the empirical record in the dossier supports substantial, human-linked climate risks. No new evidence from other panelists warrants revision.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE

evidence.text: The May 2014 National Climate Assessment report said human-caused climate changes, such as increased heat waves and drought, "are visible in every state." A Sep. 2014 American Meteorological Society study found that human-caused climate change "greatly increased" (up to 10 times) the risk for extreme heat waves in 2013. According to an Aug. 2012 study published in the , there is a "high degree of confidence" that the Texas and Oklahoma heat waves and drought of 2011, and heat waves and drought in Moscow in 2010, "were a consequence of global warming" and that "extreme anomalies" in weather are becoming more common as a direct consequence of human-caused climate change.

According to The Center For Biological Diversity , the world's climate is changing as a result of the burning of fossil fuels. The burning of fossil fuels creates carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide traps heat in the atmosphere, and this causes the world's temperature to rise. This is likely to reduce the amount of arable land on Earth, and it will cause food prices to increase. Furthermore, climate change is likely to result in rising sea levels. There even are major cities that could be flooded. As the population increases, the production of fossil fuels will increase. This is likely to result in climate change occurring at an increasingly rapid pace.

It is the sun that is the driving force of our climate and so it makes sense that it has the biggest impact on our climate rather than anything that humans might be doing. The sun is therefore the most likely cause of global warming. Professor Henrik Svensmark, a physicist at the Danish National Space Center in Copenhagen argues that climate change is caused by solar activity. Solar activity could affect climate by variation in the Sun's output or potentially through having an effect on cloud formation. Sunspot numbers and cosmic ray fluxes...

Over the past 10,000 years, solar minima (reduced sun spot activity) have been "accompanied by sharp climate changes." Between 1900 and 2000 solar irradiance increased 0.19%, and correlated with the rise in US surface temperatures over the 20th century. According to a 2007 study published in , "variations in solar activity and not the burning of fossil fuels are the direct cause of the observed multiyear variations in climatic responses." In a 2012 study by Willie Soon, PhD, Physicist at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, a strong correlation between solar radiation and temperatures in the Arctic over the past 130 years was identified.

debates.claim: The threat of Climate Change is exaggerated

text.A|1:
The strongest dossier-based case for exaggeration rests on E3 and E4: solar activity is the primary climate driver, with a 2007 study attributing multiyear climatic variations to solar variation rather than fossil fuels, and a 2012 study finding strong solar-radiation correlation with Arctic temperatures. If solar forcing dominates, projected human-caused catastrophe is overstated. Material counterevidence, however, is strong: E1 documents human-caused heat-wave risk increased up to tenfold and attributes specific droughts/heat waves to global warming; E2 warns of sea-level rise and food insecurity. These are empirical findings, not mere values. But the solar-correlation evidence directly challenges the causal basis for alarm, and the dossier lacks a direct refutation of the solar mechanism. Thus, while human influence is not disproven, the claimed severity of the threat is not established by these dossiers and appears exaggerated relative to natural variability.

VERDICT: SUPPORT
text.B|1:
The dossier's strongest countercase comes from E1 and E2. E1 documents peer-reviewed findings that human-caused climate change "greatly increased" extreme heat wave risk and that specific droughts/heat waves were "a consequence of global warming," with "extreme anomalies" becoming more common. E2 outlines concrete threats: reduced arable land, rising food prices, flooding of major cities, and accelerating change. These directly contradict the claim that the threat is exaggerated.

Material supporting the claim: E3 and E4 attribute climate change to solar activity, citing correlations between solar irradiance/sunspots and temperature. This could imply human influence is overstated. However, these sources are not peer-reviewed consensus (e.g., a physicist's argument, a 2012 study) and do not refute the documented impacts in E1/E2. Correlation with solar activity does not establish that the threat is exaggerated.

The weight of evidence shows severe, human-caused risks, not exaggeration.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE
text.C|1:
The dossier does not support the claim that the threat of climate change is exaggerated. E1 presents specific scientific findings—from the National Climate Assessment, an AMS study, and a 2012 journal study—showing human-caused climate change is already increasing heat waves, droughts, and extreme weather with high confidence. E2 describes concrete risks: rising sea levels, reduced arable land, and higher food prices. E3 and E4 offer a solar-activity alternative, but they rely on correlations and selective citations, and they do not refute the direct evidence of human-caused warming or its projected impacts. The existence of a solar hypothesis does not establish that the threat is exaggerated; it merely presents a contested cause. Overall, the evidence indicates a serious, human-driven threat, not an exaggerated one.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE
text.A|2:
The other panelists correctly anchor their assessments in E1 and E2. E1 supplies peer-reviewed, high-confidence findings that human-caused warming increased extreme heat-wave risk and contributed to specific droughts/heat waves. E2 identifies concrete, severe impacts—rising seas, reduced arable land, food-price hikes—that contradict the idea of exaggeration.

E3 and E4 support the claim only through solar-correlation arguments. But correlation is not causation, and these sources do not rebut the direct attribution evidence in E1 or the impact mechanisms in E2. A contested solar hypothesis does not demonstrate that the threat is overstated.

I see no reason to revise my position. The dossier’s weight remains against the claim.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE
text.B|2:
Panelist A’s SUPPORT relies on E3/E4, but those are correlational solar-activity findings, not causal refutations of human forcing. E4’s 0.19% irradiance increase and Arctic correlation do not explain E1’s up-to-10-fold increase in extreme heat-wave risk or its high-confidence attribution of specific droughts/heat waves to global warming. Correlation does not establish causation, and solar variability can coexist with greenhouse-gas forcing. E2’s sea-level and food-security risks are empirical projections, not mere values. While E3/E4 offer some evidence for natural variability, the dossier’s most direct evidence—E1—supports a substantial human contribution. Therefore the strongest evidence does not show the threat is exaggerated; it undermines that claim.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE
text.C|2:
Panelist A’s conclusion overreaches. E3 and E4 show correlations between solar activity and temperature, but correlation does not establish that solar forcing dominates human forcing. The asserted link “solar activity is the primary climate driver” is not established. E1 directly contradicts it, attributing specific heat waves and droughts to human-caused warming with high confidence and up to tenfold increased heat-wave risk. E2 describes plausible impact chains but is advocacy, not independent evidence.

The dossier does not establish that the threat is exaggerated. It also does not fully establish the severity of future impacts. The key missing links are: (1) solar causation versus human causation is unresolved; (2) no quantitative comparison of forcing magnitudes; (3) isolated studies are insufficient to overturn the broader attribution evidence. Thus the claim remains unproven.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
text.A|3:
Panelist B is right: E3/E4 are correlational, not causal, and cannot explain E1’s high-confidence attribution of specific heat waves and droughts to human forcing. Panelist C correctly notes the solar-versus-human question is not fully resolved and that no quantitative forcing comparison is given. But the claim under review is that the threat is exaggerated, and the dossier’s most direct evidence—E1—points the other way: up to 10-fold increased heat-wave risk and “high degree of confidence” that extreme anomalies are consequences of global warming. E2 adds plausible sea-level and food-security risks. Solar correlations do not refute those findings; they can coexist with greenhouse-gas forcing. Missing quantitative details create uncertainty about magnitude, but they do not support the assertion that the threat is exaggerated. The strongest dossier-based position is therefore to reject the claim.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE
text.B|3:
Panelist A's reasoning is sound: E1 provides direct attribution evidence—human-caused warming "greatly increased" extreme heat risk and high-confidence links to specific droughts—which directly contradicts the claim. E2 identifies concrete severe impacts like sea-level rise and reduced arable land, showing the threat is not exaggerated.

The solar-correlation evidence in E3/E4 does not overturn this. Correlations with sunspot activity and irradiance do not establish causation, and they fail to address the mechanism-based attribution in E1. A 0.19% irradiance increase over the 20th century is also not shown to account for observed warming trends.

The dossier's strongest countercase is the peer-reviewed attribution evidence in E1 and the impact mechanisms in E2. I maintain my assessment.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE
text.C|3:
Panelist A’s reasoning is sound. E1 provides direct attribution evidence: peer-reviewed studies link human-caused warming to increased extreme-heat risk and specific droughts/heat waves. E2 identifies concrete impact pathways—rising seas, reduced arable land, food-price increases—that weigh against the claim that the threat is exaggerated.

E3 and E4 do not establish the claim. They show correlations between solar activity and temperature, but correlation is not causation. They do not rebut E1’s attribution findings, nor do they show that projected impacts are overstated. The solar hypothesis remains contested and incomplete.

The asserted link that solar activity, rather than fossil-fuel emissions, explains recent warming is not established. Likewise, the claim that climate threats are exaggerated is not supported by the dossier. The weight of evidence supports the reality and seriousness of climate change.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE

evidence.text: The May 2014 National Climate Assessment report said human-caused climate changes, such as increased heat waves and drought, "are visible in every state." A Sep. 2014 American Meteorological Society study found that human-caused climate change "greatly increased" (up to 10 times) the risk for extreme heat waves in 2013. According to an Aug. 2012 study published in the , there is a "high degree of confidence" that the Texas and Oklahoma heat waves and drought of 2011, and heat waves and drought in Moscow in 2010, "were a consequence of global warming" and that "extreme anomalies" in weather are becoming more common as a direct consequence of human-caused climate change.

According to The Center For Biological Diversity , the world's climate is changing as a result of the burning of fossil fuels. The burning of fossil fuels creates carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide traps heat in the atmosphere, and this causes the world's temperature to rise. This is likely to reduce the amount of arable land on Earth, and it will cause food prices to increase. Furthermore, climate change is likely to result in rising sea levels. There even are major cities that could be flooded. As the population increases, the production of fossil fuels will increase. This is likely to result in climate change occurring at an increasingly rapid pace.

It is the sun that is the driving force of our climate and so it makes sense that it has the biggest impact on our climate rather than anything that humans might be doing. The sun is therefore the most likely cause of global warming. Professor Henrik Svensmark, a physicist at the Danish National Space Center in Copenhagen argues that climate change is caused by solar activity. Solar activity could affect climate by variation in the Sun's output or potentially through having an effect on cloud formation. Sunspot numbers and cosmic ray fluxes...

Over the past 10,000 years, solar minima (reduced sun spot activity) have been "accompanied by sharp climate changes." Between 1900 and 2000 solar irradiance increased 0.19%, and correlated with the rise in US surface temperatures over the 20th century. According to a 2007 study published in , "variations in solar activity and not the burning of fossil fuels are the direct cause of the observed multiyear variations in climatic responses." In a 2012 study by Willie Soon, PhD, Physicist at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, a strong correlation between solar radiation and temperatures in the Arctic over the past 130 years was identified.
